question: Gautama Buddha was born in the Lumbini garden under a sal tree. Lumbini is located near Kapilavastu in present-day ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Nepal.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lumbini, the birthplace of Gautama Buddha (c. 563 BC), lies near Kapilavastu, the Shakya capital, in the Terai region of present-day Nepal (लुम्बिनी, कपिलवस्तु — बुद्ध का जन्मस्थान, नेपाल)

 

• Lumbini lies in the Rupandehi district of Nepal's Terai, a short distance from the Indian border, and in the Buddha's time it belonged to the territory of the Shakya republic whose capital was Kapilavastu.

 

• According to Buddhist tradition his mother Mahamaya was travelling to her parental home when she gave birth in the Lumbini garden, standing under a sal tree.

 

• Because birth is only the first of the five great events, SSC questions frequently ask students to separate the birthplace (Nepal) from the sites of enlightenment, first sermon and death, which all lie in India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ashoka's pillar at Lumbini, discovered in the nineteenth century, carries a Brahmi inscription saying that he visited the place, that the Buddha was born there and that the village was freed from tax.

 

• Lumbini was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1997 and is in Nepal's Rupandehi district.

 

• The other four great pilgrimage centres are Bodh Gaya and Rajgir in Bihar and Sarnath and Kushinagar in Uttar Pradesh, which SSC often asks state-wise.

 

• Buddha Purnima, the full-moon day of Vaishakha, is celebrated as the day of his birth and, in the Theravada tradition, of his enlightenment and death too.

 

NOTE

 

• Bihar (Option 1): Bihar holds Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha attained enlightenment, as well as Rajagriha and Vaishali, which hosted the first two Councils. The birth garden of Lumbini, however, lies on the Nepal side of the border, so Bihar fits a different event of his life.

 

• Uttar Pradesh (Option 2): Uttar Pradesh contains Sarnath, where the first sermon was given, and Kushinagar, where he died. These are two of the five great event sites, but neither is the place of his birth.

 

• Bhutan (Option 3): Bhutan is a Himalayan kingdom whose Buddhism came much later from Tibet and belongs to the Vajrayana tradition. It has no connection with the Shakya republic or with the Buddha's birth.

question: Gautama Buddha belonged to which Gana and Varna?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shakya Gana and Kshatriya Varna.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Buddha, whose childhood name was Siddhartha, was born into the Shakya Gana and the Kshatriya Varna; his father Suddhodana headed this republican clan (शाक्य गण — क्षत्रिय वर्ण)

 

• The Shakyas were one of the republican clans (ganas) of the sixth century BC, governed by an assembly of elders with a chief; the Buddha's father Suddhodana is described in tradition as the head of this clan.

 

• Because Buddhism and Jainism both began in Kshatriya clans of eastern India, both founders came from ruling families who gave up royal comforts, a point often used in comparison questions.

 

• The Buddha's later titles Shakyamuni (sage of the Shakyas) and Shakyasimha preserve his clan name in Buddhist literature and in Mahayana worship.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kapilavastu, the Shakya capital, later came under the powerful kingdom of Kosala, whose king Prasenajit was himself a follower of the Buddha.

 

• The Licchavis, Mallas, Koliyas and Shakyas were among the best known gana-sanghas, republics ruled by assemblies, in the sixth century BC.

 

• Gautama is the clan-name form that, according to the notes, he took from his stepmother Prajapati Gautami, while Shakyamuni means the sage of the Shakyas.

 

• Both the Buddha and Mahavira were born into Kshatriya clans of the eastern Gangetic plain, and both rejected the authority of the Vedic priesthood.

 

NOTE

 

• Koliya Gana and Brahmin Varna (Option 1): The Koliyas were the neighbouring clan of the Shakyas, and the notes describe Mahamaya as a Koliya princess, so this clan was the Buddha's maternal link. He himself was a Kshatriya Shakya, not a Koliya and certainly not a Brahmin.

 

• Licchavi Gana and Vaishya Varna (Option 3): The Licchavis ruled from Vaishali as part of the Vajji confederacy and were closely connected with Mahavira's family. Vaishali also hosted the Second Buddhist Council, but the Buddha was not a Licchavi.

 

• Malla Gana and Shudra Varna (Option 4): The Mallas ruled at Kushinagar and Pava, and the Buddha died on Malla soil. That is a link with his death, not his birth, and no tradition makes him a Shudra.

question: Who raised Siddhartha after his mother Mahamaya died seven days after his birth, giving him the name 'Gautama'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Prajapati Gautami.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Prajapati Gautami, the sister of Mahamaya, raised the infant after Mahamaya died seven days after his birth, and from her the prince got the name Gautama (प्रजापति गौतमी — सौतेली माँ/मौसी)

 

• Mahamaya died only seven days after giving birth, so her younger sister Prajapati Gautami, who was also married to Suddhodana, took charge of the infant and brought him up as her own son.

 

• The notes explain that the name Gautama came to the prince through this foster mother, while Siddhartha (one who achieves his aims) was his personal name.

 

• Her role did not end with childhood: after Ananda's request she became the first woman admitted to the Sangha, which is why her name appears in two different types of SSC questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Later Buddhist tradition lists eight special rules called garudhammas that were laid down for the nuns when Prajapati Gautami and other Shakya women were ordained.

 

• The order of nuns was called the Bhikkhuni Sangha and its first member was the Buddha's foster mother.

 

• The Buddha's wife Yashodhara and his son Rahula also joined the Sangha in the tradition.

 

• Mahamaya's early death is why the notes stress the stepmother: the same woman who raised him later became the first member of the order of nuns.

 

NOTE

 

• Yashodhara (Option 1): Yashodhara was the Buddha's wife, married to him at 16 according to the notes, and mother of Rahula. She stayed in the palace after the Great Departure, so she had no part in raising the infant Siddhartha.

 

• Sujata (Option 2): Sujata was a village girl of the Bodh Gaya area who, in tradition, offered him milk-rice just before his enlightenment. Her story belongs to the period of his penance and is unrelated to his childhood.

 

• Ambapali (Option 3): Ambapali was a famous courtesan of Vaishali who gave her mango grove to the Buddha and the Sangha and later joined as a nun. She belongs to the last years of his life, not his upbringing.

question: Which of the following was NOT one of the four sights that disturbed Prince Siddhartha before his renunciation?
solution_text:
The correct answer is A victorious warrior king.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The four sights were an old man, a sick man, a dead body (corpse) and a wandering ascetic (monk); a victorious warrior king was not among them (चार दृश्य — वृद्ध, रोगी, शव, संन्यासी)

 

• The tradition says the prince, who had been kept in the palace and shielded from pain, saw an old man, a sick man and a corpse on three drives outside the city; each one revealed a form of suffering he had never known.

 

• The fourth sight, a calm wandering monk, suggested to him that a person could rise above suffering through renunciation, and this led to the Mahabhinishkramana.

 

• A victorious king belongs to the world of power and pleasure that Siddhartha was leaving behind, so it cannot be one of the sights that pushed him to renounce.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The detailed story of the four sights is told in later biographies such as Ashvaghosha's Sanskrit poem Buddhacharita, composed in the Kushana age.

 

• The first Noble Truth, that the world is full of suffering, is a direct reflection of the sights of old age, disease and death.

 

• After leaving the palace he cut off his hair, exchanged his princely clothes for simple robes and began the life of a wandering seeker.

 

• Three of the four sights show the universal facts of ageing, sickness and death, which correspond to the central Buddhist teaching that all conditioned existence involves suffering.

 

NOTE

 

• An old man (Option 1): An old man was the first sight in the tradition and showed the prince the certainty of ageing. Since it is one of the four sights, it cannot be the answer to a question that asks for the exception.

 

• A corpse (Option 3): A corpse was the third sight, which made the prince understand that death comes to everyone, rich or poor. It is part of the standard list given in the notes, so it is not the odd one out.

 

• A wandering ascetic (Option 4): A wandering ascetic was the fourth sight and the only calm one, giving the prince a model for the path of renunciation. It is included in the notes' list and therefore cannot be the exception.

question: At what age did Siddhartha leave his home in the event called Mahabhinishkramana?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 29 years.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Siddhartha left his home, wife and son at the age of 29 in the event known as Mahabhinishkramana (the Great Departure) (महाभिनिष्क्रमण — गृहत्याग, 29 वर्ष)

 

• The Mahabhinishkramana (great going forth) took place when Siddhartha was 29, after he had lived in luxury, married Yashodhara at 16 and become a father to Rahula.

 

• After leaving he spent about six years searching, so the arithmetic of the notes works: he left at 29 and attained enlightenment at 35.

 

• The horse is the symbol of this event among the five great events, and Buddhist art often shows an empty horse and an umbrella to represent his departure without showing him.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Tradition names his horse Kanthaka and his charioteer Channa, who rode with him as far as the river bank before returning to the palace.

 

• The Buddha spent about forty-five years teaching after his enlightenment at 35, until his death at 80.

 

• Jainism's founder Mahavira also left home, at the age of 30 according to tradition, a contrast that is often set in comparison questions.

 

• After leaving the palace, the prince is said to have crossed the river Anoma, cut his hair with his sword and handed his ornaments to Channa.

 

NOTE

 

• 16 years (Option 1): Sixteen is the age at which, according to the notes, he married Yashodhara. This is a family event from his palace life and happened thirteen years before he left home.

 

• 35 years (Option 2): Thirty-five is the age of his enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, reached after six years of wandering and penance. It marks the end of his search, not its beginning.

 

• 80 years (Option 3): Eighty is the age at which he died at Kushinagar, the event called Mahaparinirvana. It is the last of the five great events, so it cannot describe the Great Departure.

question: Who was the first teacher of Siddhartha, from whom he learnt meditation after leaving home?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Alara Kalama.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• After the Great Departure Siddhartha went to Alara Kalama, who became his first teacher and taught him the practice of meditation (आलार कलाम — प्रथम गुरु)

 

• Alara Kalama was a teacher of meditation whom Siddhartha approached soon after leaving home; the notes record that he became his mentor, teaching a meditative attainment that did not yet bring liberation.

 

• Dissatisfied, he turned to another teacher, Uddaka Ramaputta, and then practised severe austerities with five companions, but neither path ended his search.

 

• The sequence shows that the Buddha's enlightenment was the result of his own effort and insight at Bodh Gaya under the Bodhi tree, not the gift of a teacher.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• After rejecting extreme fasting, the prince accepted food from the village girl Sujata and formulated the Middle Path between luxury and self-torture.

 

• The five ascetic companions who had left him in disgust became the audience of his first sermon at Sarnath.

 

• The period of wandering and study under teachers lasted six years according to the notes.

 

• Uddaka Ramaputta, the second teacher in the tradition, taught a higher meditative state than Alara Kalama, but even this did not give the prince final release.

 

NOTE

 

• Moggaliputta Tissa (Option 1): Moggaliputta Tissa was the learned monk who presided over the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra under Ashoka, roughly two centuries after the Buddha. He could not have taught the young Siddhartha.

 

• Mahakasyapa (Option 2): Mahakasyapa was a senior disciple who became a leader of the Sangha and presided over the First Council at Rajagriha. He joined the Buddha only after the enlightenment, not before it.

 

• Upali (Option 4): Upali was a disciple, in tradition a former barber, remembered as the authority on monastic discipline and the reciter of the Vinaya at the First Council. He too belongs to the period after the enlightenment.

question: Gautama Buddha attained enlightenment sitting beneath a Peepal tree at Bodh Gaya on the bank of which river?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Niranjana.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Buddha attained enlightenment (Nirvana) at the age of 35 under a Peepal (Bodhi) tree at Bodh Gaya, on the bank of the Niranjana river, after intense penance (निरंजना नदी — बोधगया, ज्ञान प्राप्ति)

 

• The Buddha sat in meditation beneath a Peepal tree at Bodh Gaya, on the bank of the Niranjana river, and after intense penance attained enlightenment at 35; the tree came to be called the Bodhi (wisdom) tree.

 

• The notes explain that the title Buddha, meaning the Enlightened One or awakened one, was used for him from this moment, and the event itself is called Nirvana.

 

• The tree is the symbol of this event among the five great events, so SSC match-the-following questions pair enlightenment with tree and Bodh Gaya.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Mahabodhi Temple complex at Bodh Gaya in Bihar is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the most sacred of the Buddhist pilgrimage places.

 

• Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitra is said to have carried a branch of the Bodhi tree to Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka, where the descendant tree still stands.

 

• The Niranjana, also called the Phalgu in its lower course, is a seasonal river flowing near Gaya in Bihar.

 

• The Vajrasana, a stone seat said to mark the spot where the Buddha sat, still stands beside the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya.

 

NOTE

 

• Ganga (Option 1): The Ganga flows north of Bodh Gaya past Pataliputra and Vaishali, and is associated with the Magadhan capitals. It is not the river on whose bank the Buddha attained enlightenment.

 

• Gandak (Option 3): The Gandak flows through Nepal and north Bihar near Vaishali and the Malla country, an area connected with his last journey, not with his enlightenment in the Gaya region.

 

• Saryu (Option 4): The Saryu flows through Kosala, near Ayodhya, and is linked with the Kosalan region and Shravasti where the Buddha later spent many rainy seasons. It is far from Bodh Gaya.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Buddha's family:

1. His wife was Yashodhara.

2. His son was Rahula.

3. His father Suddhodana was the head of the Shakya clan.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Each of the three family statements holds good: Yashodhara was the Buddha's wife, Rahula was their son and Suddhodana, head of the Shakya clan, was his father (यशोधरा, राहुल, शुद्धोधन — बुद्ध का परिवार)

 

• The notes add that Siddhartha married at 16, that his mother Mahamaya of the Koliya clan died a week after his birth and that his stepmother Prajapati Gautami raised him, so family-tree questions can mix any of these facts.

 

• Rahula's birth is traditionally seen as the last tie that the prince had to break when he went out at 29 in the Mahabhinishkramana.

 

• Because each statement individually matches the notes, the only complete answer is the one that accepts all three.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rahula was later ordained as a young novice, and according to tradition Yashodhara and Prajapati Gautami also joined the Sangha as nuns.

 

• The Buddha's cousin Ananda became his personal attendant and the reciter of the Sutta at the First Council.

 

• Devadatta, another relative, is remembered in Buddhist tradition as the monk who opposed the Buddha and tried to split the Sangha.

 

• Suddhodana, Mahamaya and Prajapati Gautami are the names of the father, mother and stepmother and are often asked in direct SSC questions.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Dropping statement 3 makes the answer incomplete, because Suddhodana really was the Buddha's father and the chief of the Shakya clan; a true statement cannot be left out of a combination meant to include every correct one.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Leaving out statement 1 is a mistake, since the notes plainly name Yashodhara as the wife whom the prince married at the age of 16 and left behind when he renounced the world.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): Skipping statement 2 does not work, as the notes give Rahula as the Buddha's son; this true statement belongs in the correct combination.

question:
Match the five great events of the Buddha's life with their symbols:

(a) Birth

(b) Great Departure

(c) Enlightenment

(d) First Sermon

(i) Horse

(ii) Tree

(iii) Lotus / Bull

(iv) Wheel (Chakra)
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Birth matches lotus and bull, the Great Departure the horse, enlightenment the tree and the first sermon the wheel (chakra), while death has the stupa (बुद्ध के जीवन की पाँच घटनाएँ — कमल/बैल, घोड़ा, वृक्ष, चक्र, स्तूप)

 

• Each symbol points to a story: the wheel recalls the Dharma Chakra Parivartan at Sarnath, the tree the Bodhi tree of Bodh Gaya and the horse the animal on which he rode out of the palace.

 

• Early Buddhist artists avoided showing the Buddha as a person, so they used these emblems on stupa railings and gateways; this is the idea of aniconism explained in the notes.

 

• Only one option pairs all four correctly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The sequence of sites for the five events is Lumbini, Kapilavastu (home), Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar.

 

• Footprints (Buddhapada) and an empty throne are other aniconic symbols seen at Sanchi and Bharhut.

 

• The Ashokan lion capital of Sarnath crowns a pillar bearing a wheel, which connects the first sermon with Mauryan art.

 

• The sixth major symbol often asked is the stupa for the Mahaparinirvana, since the five great events with their five symbols form a standard exam table.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-iv, d-ii (Option 1): Giving the horse to birth, the lotus to the Great Departure and the wheel to enlightenment reverses every pair, so none of the symbols matches its event here.

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 2): A pairing that gets birth and first sermon right but swaps the other two events still fails; the horse belongs to the Great Departure and the tree to enlightenment.

 

• a-iv, b-i, c-ii, d-iii (Option 3): Allotting the wheel to birth and the lotus to the first sermon is wrong, because the wheel stands for the first sermon at Sarnath and the lotus for his birth.

question:
Consider the following statements about the death of the Buddha:

1. He died at Kushinagar, in the Malla region.

2. He died at the age of 80 after eating food offered by the blacksmith Chunda.

3. The event is called Mahaparinirvana.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Every statement about the end of the Buddha's life is accurate: he died at Kushinagar in the Malla country at the age of 80, after the meal served by the blacksmith Chunda, an event called Mahaparinirvana (महापरिनिर्वाण — कुशीनगर, चुन्द लोहार)

 

• The notes give the year as 483 BC and assign the stupa as the symbol of this last of the five great events.

 

• His death led directly to the First Buddhist Council at Rajagriha, where the monks met to preserve his teachings.

 

• Since all three statements are supported by the notes, the correct choice is the one that includes every statement.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kushinagar lies in the Kushinagar district of eastern Uttar Pradesh and has a Mahaparinirvana temple with a reclining Buddha image and a stupa.

 

• The Mallas, like the Shakyas and Licchavis, were a republican clan, and the Buddha crossed their territory on his last journey.

 

• Mahavira, in comparison, is traditionally said to have died at Pava, also in the Malla region, a point students often mix up.

 

• The Buddha's last words, according to tradition, urged his monks to strive with diligence, because all compounded things are subject to decay.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Excluding statement 3 would be wrong because the death of the Buddha is indeed called Mahaparinirvana, the final liberation of an enlightened being, so it must be counted.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Excluding statement 1 would be wrong too, because Kushinagar in the Malla region of present-day Uttar Pradesh is exactly where the notes place his death.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): Excluding statement 2 is also faulty; the notes say he died at 80 after eating the food of Chunda the blacksmith, so this statement is accurate.

question:
Consider the following statements about the first sermon of the Buddha:

1. It was delivered at Sarnath near Benares.

2. It was addressed to five disciples.

3. It was addressed to his wife Yashodhara and son Rahula.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The sermon at Sarnath near Benares was addressed to five ascetic disciples, so statements 1 and 2 are right, but statement 3 is wrong because his wife and son were not the audience; the event is the Dharma Chakra Parivartan (धर्मचक्र प्रवर्तन — सारनाथ, पाँच शिष्य)

 

• The five were Kondanna, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahanama and Assaji, the companions who had left him when he gave up extreme fasting, and they became the first monks.

 

• The sermon presented the Middle Path and the Four Noble Truths, and it was delivered in the Pali language according to the notes.

 

• The wheel is the symbol attached to this event among the five great events.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sarnath is also called Isipatana or the Deer Park (Mrigadava), and it lies a few kilometres from Varanasi.

 

• The Dhamekh Stupa and the Ashokan pillar stand at Sarnath, which is also the origin of India's national emblem.

 

• The notes say that before Sarnath he had shared some of his knowledge with two people at Gaya.

 

• The sermon is also known by the name Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta in Pali, the discourse that set the wheel of Dhamma in motion.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Accepting statement 3 spoils this choice, since Yashodhara and Rahula did not hear the first sermon; its listeners were five ascetics, and leaving out the true statement 1 makes it worse.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Here the true statement 1 about Sarnath is left out while the false statement 3 is kept, so the choice fails on both counts even though statement 2 is correct.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Taking all three statements as true cannot work because statement 3 is false; the sermon reached only the five ascetic companions at the Deer Park.

question: Which of the following was NOT one of the five disciples to whom the Buddha delivered his first sermon at Sarnath?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Upali.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Upali was not among the five; the five disciples were Kondanna, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahanama and Assaji, and Upali was a barber who later joined the Sangha (उपालि — विनय का ज्ञाता)

 

• Upali was not one of the five ascetics of Sarnath; the five were Kondanna, Vappa, Bhaddiya, Mahanama and Assaji, who had shared the Buddha's early austerities.

 

• Upali joined later, in tradition from a humble barber background, and became the chief authority on the monastic code, so he recited the Vinaya at the First Council.

 

• His example also shows the open character of the Sangha, in which social origin did not decide a monk's standing.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sariputta and Moggallana were the two chief disciples, while Ananda served as the Buddha's personal attendant for many years.

 

• Mahakasyapa led the Sangha after the Buddha's death and presided over the First Council.

 

• The five ascetics became the first Bhikshus and formed the nucleus of the Sangha.

 

• Assaji later impressed Sariputta by briefly summarising the Buddha's teaching, and this meeting brought Sariputta and Moggallana into the Sangha.

 

NOTE

 

• Kondanna (Option 1): Kondanna was the first of the five to grasp the teaching at Sarnath, so he belongs to the group named in the notes. A question asking for an exception cannot have him as its answer.

 

• Assaji (Option 2): Assaji was one of the five ascetics who heard the first sermon and he is listed in the notes. He later became the teacher through whom Sariputta first met the Dhamma, so he cannot be the odd one out.

 

• Mahanama (Option 4): Mahanama is named in the notes among the five disciples of the Deer Park sermon. Because he is a member of the group, he cannot be the exception here.

question: The first of the Four Noble Truths (Arya Satya) taught by the Buddha is that:
option_1: The world is full of suffering
option_2: Desire is the cause of suffering
option_3: Suffering can be ended by removing desire
option_4: The Eightfold Path leads to the end of suffering
solution_text:
The correct answer is The world is full of suffering.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first Noble Truth is that the world is full of suffering (dukkha), which is the starting point of Buddha's philosophy (चार आर्य सत्य — दुःख है)

 

• The first Noble Truth (dukkha) says that life is full of suffering; the four truths run in order as suffering, cause (desire), cessation (removal of desire) and the path (Eightfold Path).

 

• The Buddha is often compared to a physician who first identifies the disease, then its cause, then declares that a cure is possible and finally prescribes the treatment.

 

• These truths formed the core of the sermon at Sarnath and are the basis of the Dhamma, the second jewel of the Tri Ratna.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• In Pali the four truths are called dukkha, samudaya, nirodha and magga.

 

• The goal of Buddhism, Nirvana, is the extinction of desire, hatred and ignorance, not a heaven in the Vedic sense.

 

• The Buddha avoided metaphysical debates on the soul and the origin of the world and kept his teaching practical.

 

• The Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path together are sometimes called the heart of the Dhamma and appear in every Buddhist school.

 

NOTE

 

• Desire is the cause of suffering (Option 2): Desire as the cause of suffering is the second Noble Truth. It follows the statement that life is suffering and explains why suffering arises, so it cannot be the first.

 

• Suffering can be ended by removing desire (Option 3): Ending suffering by removing desire is the third Noble Truth, the truth of cessation. It depends on the first two and offers hope of liberation, but comes third in the order.

 

• The Eightfold Path leads to the end of suffering (Option 4): The Eightfold Path as the means to end suffering is the fourth and last Noble Truth. It is the practical prescription that follows the diagnosis, not the starting point.

question: According to the Buddha, which of the following is the root cause of human suffering?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Desire (craving).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Buddha taught that desire (tanha, craving) is the cause of suffering; when desire is removed, suffering ends and Nirvana is attained (तृष्णा — दुःख का मूल कारण)

 

• The Buddha traced suffering to desire or craving (tanha) for pleasure, possessions and continued existence; removing this craving removes suffering and leads to Nirvana.

 

• This is the second Noble Truth, and its practical remedy is the Eightfold Path of right view, resolve, speech, conduct, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration.

 

• By locating the cause inside the human mind, Buddhism rejected explanations through fate, divine will or the performance of sacrifices.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• In Buddhist thought craving is linked with ignorance in a chain of causation that keeps the cycle of birth and death going.

 

• Nirvana literally means the blowing out of the fire of desire.

 

• The Buddha also accepted the law of karma, the idea that a person's deeds shape future births.

 

• The Buddha pointed out that suffering has three kinds of craving behind it: craving for sense pleasure, craving for existence and craving for non-existence.

 

NOTE

 

• Fate (Option 1): Fate is not the Buddha's explanation of suffering. He held that people's own craving and actions produce suffering and that they can end it by effort, which is a view opposed to fatalism, though the Ajivika sect held a doctrine of strict destiny.

 

• Sin of previous kings (Option 2): The sins of previous kings have no place in the Four Noble Truths. The Buddha explained suffering through craving, not through political events or rulers' deeds.

 

• Lack of sacrifices (Option 3): A lack of sacrifices cannot be the cause because the Buddha rejected the Vedic sacrifices as costly and useless for ending suffering. His message was ethical and mental discipline instead.

question: Which of the following is NOT a part of the Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga) of the Buddha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Right penance.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Right penance is not part of the Eightfold Path; the eight are right view, right resolve, right speech, right conduct, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration (अष्टांगिक मार्ग)

 

• Right penance is not an element of the Eightfold Path; the eight limbs are right view, resolve, speech, conduct, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration.

 

• The Buddha had tried severe austerities himself and found them useless, so his path is called the Middle Path between sensual indulgence and extreme self-torture.

 

• The eight limbs are commonly grouped as wisdom (view, resolve), morality (speech, conduct, livelihood) and mental discipline (effort, mindfulness, concentration).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jainism stressed severe penance and fasting, including the vow of sallekhana, which forms a clear contrast with the Buddhist Middle Path.

 

• The Jain Triratna (right faith, right knowledge, right conduct) should not be confused with the Buddhist Eightfold Path.

 

• The Eightfold Path is the fourth of the Four Noble Truths and leads to Nirvana.

 

• The Eightfold Path is divided into three groups: wisdom (right view, resolve), ethical conduct (speech, action, livelihood) and mental discipline (effort, mindfulness, concentration).

 

NOTE

 

• Right livelihood (Option 1): Right livelihood is the fifth limb, which asks a follower to earn a living without cheating or harming living beings. Because it is a real part of the path, it cannot be the exception.

 

• Right mindfulness (Option 3): Right mindfulness is the seventh limb, which means constant awareness of body, feelings and thoughts. It is one of the eight steps and therefore cannot be the answer.

 

• Right concentration (Option 4): Right concentration is the eighth limb and refers to deep meditation. It completes the path and is named in the notes, so it is not the exception.

question:
Consider the following statements about the teachings of the Buddha:

1. He taught the Middle Path, avoiding both luxury and extreme penance.

2. He accepted caste-based hierarchy and Vedic sacrifices.

3. He emphasised ethical conduct as the way to end suffering.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Buddha taught the Middle Path and stressed ethical conduct through the Eightfold Path, which makes statements 1 and 3 correct, while statement 2 is false because he rejected caste hierarchy and Vedic sacrifices (मध्यम मार्ग — सदाचार, जाति-भेद का विरोध)

 

• Open admission to the Sangha without caste restrictions is stated in the notes and is the textual proof against the claim that he accepted birth-based hierarchy.

 

• The simple, ethical message in a popular language attracted merchants, artisans and women, who had a low place in the Vedic order.

 

• Because one statement is false, any combination containing statement 2 has to be discarded.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Buddha preached in the language of the people, in contrast to the Sanskrit of the Vedic priests.

 

• Merchants and craftsmen supported the new religions because the Vedic order gave them a low rank.

 

• Buddhism had no creator god and no ritual priesthood.

 

• The Buddha's emphasis on rational inquiry and avoiding extremes is seen in his advice to the Kalamas that people should test teachings by experience and not accept them on authority alone.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Statement 2 is false and statement 1 is true, so a pair that contains statement 2 and omits statement 1 fails twice; the Buddha neither accepted caste hierarchy nor withheld the Middle Path.

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 2): A pair that keeps the false statement 2 and drops the correct statement 3 about ethical conduct cannot stand, even though statement 1 in it is correct.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Treating all three as correct overlooks that statement 2 contradicts the open Sangha, which took in men and women of every caste.

question:
Assertion (A): Buddhism spread quickly among common people in the age of its founder.

Reason (R): The Sangha was open to all, with no caste restrictions, and the Buddha taught in the language of the people.
option_1: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both are true and R explains A: the Sangha admitted anyone, man or woman, without caste restrictions, and the Buddha preached in the common language (Pali), so the teaching reached ordinary people (बौद्ध धर्म का तीव्र प्रसार — संघ में जातिगत भेद नहीं)

 

• Both statements are true and R explains A: the Sangha was open to all men and women regardless of caste, and the teachings were given in the language of the people, so common folk found it easy to follow.

 

• The Buddha had two kinds of followers, the monks (Bhikshus) in the Sangha and lay worshippers (Upasikas), which gave the movement a wide social base.

 

• Royal support from kings such as Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and later Ashoka then accelerated its spread.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Pali, the language of the early canon, was close to the speech of Magadha and carried the Buddha's message to common listeners.

 

• Ashoka sent Buddhist missionaries to Sri Lanka, Central Asia and the Hellenistic kingdoms mentioned in his Rock Edict XIII.

 

• Jainism, in contrast, remained largely confined to India for a long time.

 

• Ajatashatru and Prasenajit, kings of Magadha and Kosala, were among the royal patrons who supported the early growth of the Sangha.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): This option is wrong because the reason really does explain the assertion. The open Sangha and use of a popular language are the main causes of the rapid popularity, so R is not an unrelated true fact.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): This option calls the reason false, but the notes clearly state that anyone, man or woman, could join the Sangha without caste restrictions, and that the Buddha used the people's language, so R is true.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): This option calls the assertion false, but Buddhism did gain followers quickly among ordinary people, and the royal patronage of Magadhan kings helped it. A is therefore true.

question: The 'Tri Ratna' (Three Jewels) of Buddhism are:
option_1: Right view, right speech and right conduct
solution_text:
The correct answer is Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Tri Ratna (Three Jewels) of Buddhism are Buddha (the founder), Dhamma (his teachings) and Sangha (the order of monks and nuns) (त्रिरत्न — बुद्ध, धम्म, संघ)

 

• The Tri Ratna are the Buddha (the founder), the Dhamma (his teachings) and the Sangha (the order of monks and nuns), in which a follower takes refuge.

 

• Right view, speech and conduct belong to the Eightfold Path, whereas the Pitakas are the canon, so each of the other options describes a different Buddhist grouping.

 

• The Buddhist Tri Ratna must also be distinguished from the Jain Triratna of right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The three refuges are recited by laypeople when they accept the five precepts, such as abstaining from killing and stealing.

 

• Tri-Pitaka means three baskets and is the name for the Buddhist canon, which is a separate triad.

 

• Dhamma is the Pali form of the Sanskrit word Dharma.

 

• The sequence of the three jewels, Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, is repeated in the Pali formula of taking refuge, which each of the lines begins with 'I go to'.

 

NOTE

 

• Right view, right speech and right conduct (Option 1): Right view, speech and conduct are three limbs of the Eightfold Path, which describes the practice that ends suffering. They are not the Three Jewels, which are objects of refuge.

 

• Birth, enlightenment and death (Option 3): Birth, enlightenment and death are three of the five great events of the Buddha's life. They are biographical milestones and not the three jewels of the faith.

 

• Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma (Option 4): Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma are the three baskets of the Tripitaka, the Pali canon. They are texts, whereas the Three Jewels are the Buddha, the teachings and the community.

question: The two kinds of followers of the Buddha were:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bhikshus (monks) and Upasakas/Upasikas (lay worshippers).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Buddha had monks (Bhikshus) and lay worshippers (Upasakas/Upasikas) as followers; the monks were organised into the Sangha (भिक्षु और उपासक/उपासिका)

 

• The Buddha had monks (Bhikshus), who joined the Sangha and lived on alms, and lay worshippers (Upasakas and Upasikas), who supported them with food and gifts while following the five precepts.

 

• The Sangha was open to men and women of every caste, which made this twofold community more inclusive than the Vedic order.

 

• The rules for monks and nuns were collected in the Vinaya Pitaka.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Monks stayed in viharas during the rainy season, which later grew into the great monasteries and centres of learning such as Nalanda.

 

• Women in the Sangha were called Bhikkhunis.

 

• Anathapindika and Ambapali are famous lay donors who gave a monastery and a mango grove to the Sangha.

 

• The Upasakas and Upasikas observed five precepts, whereas the monks and nuns followed a much larger number of rules in the Vinaya.

 

NOTE

 

• Brahmins and Kshatriyas (Option 1): Brahmins and Kshatriyas are social classes of the varna system, not types of Buddhist followers. Followers came from all varnas, and the Buddha himself was a Kshatriya.

 

• Sthaviras and Mahasanghikas (Option 2): Sthaviras and Mahasanghikas are the two sects into which the Sangha divided after the Second Council. They describe schools of monks, not the two classes of followers.

 

• Shramanas and Grihastas only (Option 3): Shramana is a general term for wandering ascetics of many sects, including Jains, and Grihastas are householders of the Brahmanical scheme. Neither is the specific Buddhist pair.

question: Who requested the Buddha to allow women into the Sangha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ananda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• It was Ananda, the Buddha's close disciple and cousin, who requested the Buddha to admit women into the Sangha, and the Buddha agreed (आनन्द — स्त्रियों के प्रवेश का अनुरोध)

 

• Ananda, the Buddha's cousin and constant attendant, asked the Buddha to admit women into the Sangha, and the Buddha agreed; the first woman admitted was his stepmother Prajapati Gautami.

 

• Ananda was known for his excellent memory, so he recited the Sutta at the First Council after the Buddha's death.

 

• His plea is evidence of the Sangha's openness to women, an important feature to remember in SSC statement questions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ananda is said to have attained arhatship just before the First Council began, after which he was allowed to take part in it.

 

• Upali recited the Vinaya at the same council.

 

• SSC recently asked about the significance of Ananda in Buddhist tradition in a Delhi Police paper.

 

• Because Ananda had asked on women's behalf, the nuns' order gave a new religious opportunity to women of all classes, as seen in the Therigatha poems.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahakasyapa (Option 1): Mahakasyapa was the senior monk who presided over the First Council and led the Sangha after the Buddha's death. He was not the disciple who interceded for women.

 

• Upali (Option 2): Upali was the disciple known as the master of the monastic code and the reciter of the Vinaya at the First Council. He did not make the request.

 

• Ajatashatru (Option 4): Ajatashatru was the Magadhan king who patronised the First Council. As a royal patron, he did not plead for women's admission.

question: Who was the first woman to be admitted to the Buddhist Sangha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Prajapati Gautami.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Prajapati Gautami, the Buddha's stepmother and maternal aunt, was the first woman admitted to the Buddhist Sangha after Ananda pleaded on behalf of women (प्रजापति गौतमी — प्रथम भिक्षुणी)

 

• Prajapati Gautami, the Buddha's stepmother, was the first woman admitted to the Sangha after Ananda's request, and she became the first of the Bhikkhunis.

 

• She had raised him after Mahamaya's death and, according to tradition, led a group of Shakya women to ask for ordination.

 

• Her admission shows that the Sangha accepted women, though with additional rules, which contrasted with the Vedic ritual tradition.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Admission of women was a sharp break from the Vedic ritual tradition, in which women had little religious role.

 

• Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitra later became a nun and took the Bodhi sapling to Sri Lanka.

 

• Women monks of Buddhism were called Bhikkhunis, and monks Bhikkhus.

 

• The Therigatha, a Pali text of verses by the early nuns, is an important source for women's religious life in ancient India.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahamaya (Option 1): Mahamaya was the Buddha's mother and died seven days after his birth, long before the Sangha was formed. She could not have been its first woman member.

 

• Ambapali (Option 2): Ambapali was a courtesan of Vaishali who donated her mango grove to the Sangha and later became a nun. She belongs to a later period and was not the first woman admitted.

 

• Sanghamitra (Option 3): Sanghamitra was Ashoka's daughter, who lived about two centuries after the Buddha and carried Buddhism to Sri Lanka. She is a Mauryan-age figure and not the first member.

question: The First Buddhist Council was held at which place immediately after the death of the Buddha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajagriha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The First Buddhist Council was held at Rajagriha in the Saptaparni cave soon after the Buddha's death, under the patronage of Ajatashatru (राजगृह — प्रथम बौद्ध संगीति, सप्तपर्णी गुफा)

 

• The First Buddhist Council met at Rajagriha, in the Saptaparni cave, soon after the Buddha's death in 483 BC; Ajatashatru organised it and Mahakasyapa presided.

 

• The monks wanted to preserve the teachings, so Upali recited the Vinaya and Ananda the Sutta, which form the base of the Tripitaka.

 

• Rajagriha was then the Magadhan capital, and this royal patronage explains why the first council met there.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rajagriha (Rajgir) was the early capital of Magadha before Pataliputra and is ringed by five hills.

 

• Ajatashatru belonged to the Haryanka dynasty and was a contemporary of both the Buddha and Mahavira.

 

• The Second Council took place a century later at Vaishali.

 

• The Sattapanni (Saptaparni) cave at Rajagriha is situated on the Vaibhara hill, which is still visited by Buddhist pilgrims.

 

NOTE

 

• Vaishali (Option 2): Vaishali was the venue of the Second Council, held about a century later under Kalashoka to settle disputes over monastic rules. It is therefore not the place of the first meeting.

 

• Pataliputra (Option 3): Pataliputra hosted the Third Council under Ashoka around 250 BC, more than two centuries after the first. It was the Mauryan capital, not Rajagriha, the site of the first meeting.

 

• Kundalavana (Option 4): Kundalavana near Srinagar in Kashmir was the site of the Fourth Council under Kanishka in the Kushana period. It is far later and far away from the first council.

question: Who presided over the First Buddhist Council held at Rajagriha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mahakasyapa.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahakasyapa (Mahakassapa), a leading disciple of the Buddha, was the chairman of the First Buddhist Council held at Rajagriha (महाकश्यप — प्रथम संगीति के अध्यक्ष)

 

• Mahakasyapa, a senior disciple known for strict discipline, presided over the First Council at Rajagriha, which Ajatashatru supported.

 

• Under him Upali recited the Vinaya and Ananda the Sutta, so the first two baskets of the canon trace their origin to this assembly.

 

• Matching chairmen with councils is a common question, so remember the sequence Mahakasyapa, Subhakami, Moggaliputta Tissa and Vasumitra.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahakasyapa led the Sangha after the Buddha's death and was known for his strict ascetic habits.

 

• The Abhidhamma Pitaka is associated with the Third Council, not the first.

 

• The cave site at Rajgir is called Saptaparni in the notes.

 

• The place of Mahakasyapa in the Sangha is shown by the tradition that he was chosen to lead the community after the Buddha's passing.

 

NOTE

 

• Subhakami (Option 1): Subhakami (Sabakami) presided over the Second Council at Vaishali about a century later. Since he belongs to that later council, he cannot have chaired the first.

 

• Moggaliputta Tissa (Option 2): Moggaliputta Tissa chaired the Third Council at Pataliputra in Ashoka's reign, roughly 250 BC, so he lived about two centuries after the first council.

 

• Vasumitra (Option 4): Vasumitra chaired the Fourth Council under Kanishka at Kundalavana in Kashmir, in the Kushana age, which is many centuries after the first council.

question: The Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali was organised by which ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kalashoka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali (383 BC) was organised by Kalashoka (Kakavarna) of the Shishunaga dynasty, with Subhakami as chairman (कालाशोक — द्वितीय संगीति, वैशाली)

 

• Kalashoka (Kakavarna) of the Shishunaga dynasty organised the Second Council at Vaishali in 383 BC; the council met under Subhakami to settle the disputes about monastic rules.

 

• The meeting is remembered for the Vajjian monks of Vaishali, whose ten practices were judged by the strict monks to be against the Vinaya.

 

• The differences led to the division into Sthaviravadins and Mahasanghikas, as stated in the notes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kalashoka should not be confused with the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, who lived much later.

 

• The Shishunagas came after the Haryankas and were followed by the Nandas in Magadha.

 

• SSC has asked this fact in the form 'during whose reign was the second Buddhist council held'.

 

• After the Vaishali council Buddhism's elders are said to have declared the Vajjian monks' ten practices unlawful.

 

NOTE

 

• Ajatashatru (Option 2): Ajatashatru was a Haryanka king who patronised the First Council at Rajagriha, about a century before the Vaishali council. He belongs to an earlier dynasty than Kalashoka.

 

• Ashoka (Option 3): Ashoka was the Mauryan emperor who organised the Third Council at Pataliputra around 250 BC. Since he came after Kalashoka by over a century, he was not the patron of the Second.

 

• Kanishka (Option 4): Kanishka was the Kushana ruler of the first-second centuries AD and patron of the Fourth Council. He lived many centuries after the Second Council.

question: Buddhism split into two schools, Sthaviravadins and Mahasanghikas, as a result of the:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Second Buddhist Council.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali led to the division of Buddhism into Sthaviravadins and Mahasanghikas (स्थविरवादी और महासांघिक — द्वितीय संगीति)

 

• The Second Council at Vaishali is the one that ended with the division of the Sangha into Sthaviravadins (followers of the elders) and Mahasanghikas (the great assembly).

 

• The cause was disagreement about monastic discipline, in which the strict elders opposed the more liberal practices of the Vajjian monks.

 

• The notes say these two groups later came to be known as Hinayana and Mahayana, a simplified statement of a long process of development.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Theravada Buddhism of Sri Lanka and South-East Asia descends from the Sthavira line.

 

• Mahayana ideas were developed in the Kushana period, with the works of Ashvaghosha and Nagarjuna.

 

• Later schools include Sarvastivada and Vajrayana.

 

• The Mahasanghika emphasis on the supramundane nature of the Buddha is often seen as an early step towards Mahayana ideas.

 

NOTE

 

• First Buddhist Council (Option 1): The First Council at Rajagriha collected the Buddha's sayings and the monastic rules. No split occurred there, because the Sangha was united under Mahakasyapa.

 

• Third Buddhist Council (Option 2): The Third Council under Ashoka concerned the purification of the Sangha and the preparation of the Abhidhamma, and it followed Moggaliputta Tissa. The first schism had happened earlier.

 

• Fourth Buddhist Council (Option 4): The Fourth Council in Kashmir under Kanishka is linked in the notes with the rise of Mahayana. The first split into the two schools had occurred at Vaishali long before.
